name_zh: 里希哈特茶园大吉岭红茶
cultivar: Chinary lots are sold under the name; bushes vary across the garden.
processing: Certified bio-organic Darjeeling, with orthodox making typical of the district. Oxidation depends on the flush.
harvest_season: Summer Chinary lots are sold under this name; as elsewhere in Darjeeling, picking runs through distinct seasonal flushes.
appearance_dry: Typically dark olive to brown twisted leaf, with browner tones in summer lots.
appearance_liquor: Amber in summer lots, paler in spring tea.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown with green pieces, greener in spring.
taste_profile: The garden's own cup is little described. Typical of summer China-bush Darjeeling, expect ripe fruit and a rounded sweetness, with lighter florals in spring.

brewing.notes: Summer lots take hotter water than spring ones. Western-style is the usual way.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, often with the bush type named, as in "Summer Chinary". Current-season lots are usual, and summer tea holds a little longer than spring.
description:
Rishihat, also spelled Risheehat, is a certified organic Darjeeling garden about 14 km from Darjeeling town, with Arya and Chongtong nearby. It has about 256 hectares, on slopes between roughly 760 and 1,460 metres, a lower range than some famous neighbours.

Its terrain is described as the steepest around, with rich soil. Summer Chinary lots show up in shops, meaning China-type bushes picked in the second flush, the season that goes furthest toward a full black tea.

Detailed notes on its cup are scarce. As is typical of summer China-bush Darjeeling, look for fruit and a soft sweetness, and give it a little hotter water than you would a spring tea.

The label spelling is usually Risheehat, so search both forms. A stated flush and bush type is a good sign of a careful seller.
history:
The place was first known as Tsering Bagan, after the Tserings living there. British planters set up a garden in the 1900s, and it was later renamed Rishihat, meaning home of holy sages. Jay Shree Tea acquired it in 1955.

Liza Hill was a separate estate with its own factory until 1963, after which it became a division of Rishihat.
